title: Efficient Calculation of Equilibrium Correlation Functions
authors: Yizhi Shen, Roel Van Beeumen, Wibe A. de Jong, Efekan Kökcü
abstract: A majority of measurable dynamic quantities of a physical system is described as an equilibrium correlation function of the form $G_{AB}(t-t') = \left<A(t)B(t')\right>$, where $t'$ represents the impact time and $t$ represents the response time. Conventional quantum algorithms to compute such quantities via Hamiltonian simulation such as the Hadamard test, variational methods, or linear-response-based algorithms share one feature in common: each time point $t-t'$ is calculated by a different quantum circuit, leading to at least $O(N_t)$ total shots, and at least $O(N_t^2)$ total quantum gates. Here, we provide a different approach: utilizing $O(\log N_t)$ ancilla qubits to store time as a quantum variable, and effectively parallelize the computation of an equilibrium correlation function by requiring only a single quantum circuit for all time points. We show that this circuit needs to be run only $O(\log N_t)$ times, which in total requires $O(N_t \log N_t)$ quantum resources in the large system size limits. We prove that this scaling is optimal, and demonstrate our algorithm calculating the Green's function of a one-dimensional spinless Hubbard model.
summary: This paper introduces a quantum algorithm to calculate equilibrium correlation functions by encoding time into a quantum clock register. This technique allows all time lags to be computed simultaneously using a single circuit run, achieving an optimal resource scaling of $O(N_t \log N_t)$. This drastically improves upon previous methods, making the simulation of dynamic properties in many-body systems much more efficient.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently calculating equilibrium correlation functions, $G_{AB}(t-t') = \langle A(t)B(t') angle$, which are crucial for describing measurable dynamic quantities in many-body physics.
main_result: The authors propose a novel quantum algorithm that achieves an optimal resource scaling of $O(N_t \log N_t)$ quantum resources, significantly outperforming conventional methods that require $O(N_t^2)$ gates.
method: The core method involves encoding the time evolution history into a quantum 'clock register' using $\mathcal{O}(\log N_t)$ ancilla qubits, allowing all time lags to be computed simultaneously via a single circuit run followed by a Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT).
model_or_system: The method is demonstrated using the Green's function calculation for a one-dimensional spinless Hubbard model, applicable to any system in a stationary state.
key_observables: Equilibrium correlation functions, $G_{AB}(t-t')$, autocorrelation functions, and the spectral function derived from the QFT measurement.
important_parameters: The time window size $N_t$ (number of time points) and the required accuracy $\epsilon$. The scaling advantage is most pronounced for large $N_t$.
main_assumptions: The method relies on the time-translational invariance of equilibrium correlation functions (Toeplitz form) and assumes the system is in a stationary state.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the circuit structures for the Hadamard test versus the clock circuit. Figure 3 compares the maximum estimation error for both protocols, showing the clock approach's superior scaling for large $N_t$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the computational bottleneck of conventional methods. It then introduces the clock-register approach, detailing the circuit structure and the use of QFT for readout. Finally, it rigorously compares the resource scaling and demonstrates the superior performance using the Hubbard model.
why_interesting: This work provides a significant algorithmic improvement for calculating fundamental quantities in condensed matter theory, directly impacting how quantum simulations of thermal or equilibrium dynamics can be performed on near-term quantum hardware.
